lesson.title: How Big Is the Wave? Peak, Peak-to-Peak, and RMS
lesson.summary: Amplitude describes the size of a sinusoidal voltage or current, but size can mean several different things depending on whether you care about the peak value, the full swing, or the equivalent heating effect.
lesson.body:
Up to this point, voltage and current have mostly been discussed as fixed DC quantities, or as transient exponentials settling toward a fixed value. AC signals add a new wrinkle: a sinusoidal voltage or current is constantly changing, described by v(t) = Vm*sin(omega*t + phi), so asking what the voltage is no longer has a single obvious answer. The amplitude, Vm, is the peak value the wave reaches, the height of the sine wave above its zero crossing, and it is the starting point for describing how big any AC signal really is.

But peak value is only one way to measure size, and it is not always the most useful one. The peak-to-peak value, Vpp = 2*Vm, measures the full vertical swing from the most negative point to the most positive point, which matters when you need to know how much voltage range a circuit must tolerate, such as sizing an amplifier's supply rails. The root-mean-square value, Vrms = Vm/sqrt(2) for a pure sinusoid, answers a different question entirely: it is the equivalent steady DC voltage that would deliver the same average heating power to a resistor as the AC signal actually does. All three, peak, peak-to-peak, and RMS, describe the same wave, but they are not interchangeable, and using the wrong one in a calculation is a common source of error.

RMS matters most when power is involved, because average power delivered to a resistor is P = Vrms^2/R, not Vm^2/R. This is also the convention used almost everywhere AC voltages are labeled in daily life: when a wall outlet is rated at a certain voltage, or a multimeter displays an AC reading, that number is the RMS value, not the peak, precisely because RMS is what determines how much real power the source can deliver.

A standard North American wall outlet illustrates all three quantities at once. Its voltage is commonly written as v(t) = 170*sin(377*t) V. Reading directly off this expression, the amplitude is Vm = 170 V, and the angular frequency is omega = 377 rad/s, which corresponds to a frequency f = omega/(2*pi) = 377/6.2832 = 60.0 Hz, confirming standard US mains frequency, with a period T = 1/60 = 16.67 ms. The RMS value is Vrms = 170/sqrt(2) = 170/1.4142 = 120.2 V, which is exactly why this outlet is called 120 volts even though the wire's instantaneous voltage actually swings all the way up to 170 V and back down to negative 170 V on every cycle. The peak-to-peak value is Vpp = 2*170 = 340 V, the true total swing an insulation rating or a rectifier circuit downstream would need to handle.

The amplitude concept generalizes directly to current, i(t) = Im*sin(omega*t + phi), with the same peak, peak-to-peak, and RMS relationships holding. Getting comfortable with these distinctions now, while the signals are still simple sine waves built on nothing more than the basic definitions of voltage and current, is what makes later AC power and filter calculations straightforward instead of a constant source of factor-of-1.414 errors.
